stem:
On a busy acute medical take, the nutrition nurse asks the foundation doctor which of the newly admitted people needs the most cautious introduction of feeding, with thiamine cover and daily checks of phosphate, potassium and magnesium.

Which of these patients is most likely to develop refeeding syndrome?

options.A: A 30-year-old man with obesity who began a supervised weight-loss programme a week ago
options.B: A heavy drinker aged 49 who has lost weight and barely eaten for a fortnight
options.C: A fit 25-year-old woman who has fasted overnight before an elective hernia repair
options.D: A 40-year-old woman with well-controlled type 2 diabetes admitted with cellulitis
options.E: A 70-year-old man admitted overnight after day-case cataract surgery

correct_answer: B. A heavy drinker aged 49 who has lost weight and barely eaten for a fortnight
why_correct: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is restarted after a period of starvation, causing insulin-driven shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. The highest risk lies with people who have had little or no intake for more than a few days alongside significant weight loss, especially with alcohol misuse, which also causes thiamine deficiency. He needs feeding started slowly with thiamine and close electrolyte monitoring, in line with NICE nutrition support guidance. Source: Nutrition support for adults: oral nutrition support, enteral tube feeding and parenteral nutrition (CG32), NICE, 2006, updated 2017.
why_wrong: A. A modest calorie deficit in someone with obesity does not deplete intracellular stores. C. An overnight fast in a well-nourished person carries no meaningful risk. D. Well-controlled diabetes with a short illness is not a risk factor on its own. E. A brief admission after minor surgery does not involve prolonged starvation.
pearl: NICE defines high refeeding risk as one major criterion (such as very low BMI, marked recent unintentional weight loss, little or no intake for more than 10 days, or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding) or two lesser criteria, one of which can be a history of alcohol misuse.
thinking: Who has prolonged poor intake? ↓ Significant weight loss ↓ Alcohol dependence adds thiamine and electrolyte depletion ↓ Feeding will shift electrolytes into cells ↓ Highest refeeding risk
exam_trap: A, The man with obesity on a weight-loss programme — dieting sounds like restricted intake, but he has ample body stores and has not been starved.
takeaway: Refeeding syndrome risk is greatest after prolonged minimal intake with significant weight loss, particularly in alcohol dependence.
notes: Reviewer fix: Pearl corrected: NICE refeeding risk = one major criterion or two lesser ones (alcohol misuse is a lesser criterion), replacing inaccurate 'fewer criteria needed with alcohol'

stem:
A 44-year-old woman awaiting pituitary surgery for Cushing's disease tells the endocrine nurse that she can no longer lift her arms to hang the washing on the line and needs to push on her knees to get up from a low sofa. Her hands feel strong and she has no numbness.

Which neuromuscular finding is most likely on examination?

options.A: Distal sensory loss in a stocking distribution

why_correct: Excess cortisol causes muscle protein breakdown and a myopathy that mainly affects the large proximal muscles of the hips and shoulders. This explains her difficulty raising her arms and standing from a low seat while her hand strength remains normal. The weakness usually improves once cortisol levels are brought under control. Source: Cushing's syndrome: symptoms, NHS website, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Stocking sensory loss is a feature of peripheral neuropathy, and she has no numbness. B. Fasciculations with brisk reflexes suggest motor neurone disease. C. A pill-rolling tremor indicates parkinsonism. D. Fatigable ptosis and diplopia suggest myasthenia gravis.
pearl: Long-term high-dose prednisolone causes the same steroid myopathy as endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
thinking: Cushing's disease ↓ Cannot lift arms or rise from a low seat ↓ Hand strength preserved ↓ Cortisol excess causes muscle catabolism ↓ Proximal myopathy
exam_trap: D, Fatigable ptosis and double vision — myasthenia also causes weakness, but it typically affects eye muscles and fatigues with use, which is not the picture here.
takeaway: Cortisol excess causes a symmetrical proximal myopathy.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman on the surgical ward is reviewed the morning after a total thyroidectomy for Graves' disease because she has pins and needles in her fingertips. When the nurse inflates a blood pressure cuff on her upper arm, her wrist flexes and her fingers stiffen and extend, and the spasm releases only when the cuff is deflated.

Which clinical sign has been demonstrated?
why_correct: Inflating a cuff above systolic pressure causes ischaemia of the forearm nerves, which in hypocalcaemia triggers carpal spasm with wrist flexion and finger extension. This is Trousseau's sign. After thyroidectomy it most often reflects damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands, and her calcium should be checked urgently. Source: Emergency management of acute hypocalcaemia in adult patients, Society for Endocrinology, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Chvostek's sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped. B. Brudzinski's sign is reflex flexion of the hips and knees when the neck is flexed, seen in meningism. C. Murphy's sign is arrest of inspiration on palpating the gallbladder. D. Babinski's sign is an extensor plantar response from an upper motor neurone lesion.
pearl: Trousseau's sign is more specific for hypocalcaemia than Chvostek's sign, which can be present in a minority of people with normal calcium.
thinking: Post-thyroidectomy ↓ Peripheral tingling ↓ Cuff inflation induces carpal spasm ↓ Neuromuscular irritability from low calcium ↓ Trousseau's sign
exam_trap: A, Chvostek's sign — both signs indicate hypocalcaemia and are often confused, but Chvostek's involves tapping the face rather than inflating a cuff.
takeaway: Carpal spasm provoked by inflating a blood pressure cuff is Trousseau's sign of hypocalcaemia.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman sees her GP with a year of slowly increasing tiredness, weight gain and constipation. Her neck has become fuller, and examination finds a firm, rubbery, non-tender diffuse goitre. Blood tests show a raised TSH and a low free T4. She lives in the UK and eats a normal diet.

What is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A firm, diffuse, painless goitre with gradually developing primary hypothyroidism is the typical presentation of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the gland causes the goitre and progressive loss of thyroid hormone production. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually strongly positive, and treatment is with levothyroxine. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023; Underactive thyroid: causes, NHS website, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Graves disease causes hyperthyroidism, not low free T4. B. De Quervain thyroiditis causes a painful tender gland after a viral illness, usually with an initial thyrotoxic phase. C. Toxic multinodular goitre causes hyperthyroidism with a nodular gland. E. Iodine deficiency is the commonest cause worldwide but rare in the UK with a normal diet.
pearl: Hashimoto thyroiditis carries a small increased risk of primary thyroid lymphoma, so a rapidly enlarging goitre in a patient with this condition needs urgent assessment.
thinking: Gradual hypothyroid symptoms ↓ Firm, rubbery, painless diffuse goitre ↓ High TSH with low free T4 ↓ Iodine-sufficient UK setting ↓ Autoimmune Hashimoto thyroiditis
exam_trap: A, Graves disease — it is the best known autoimmune thyroid disease with a diffuse goitre, but it causes an overactive gland rather than hypothyroidism.
takeaway: In iodine-sufficient countries, Hashimoto thyroiditis is the commonest cause of hypothyroidism with a goitre.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with palpitations. Over the past two months she has lost weight despite a good appetite, feels hot when others are comfortable, and has a fine tremor of her outstretched hands. Her ECG shows atrial fibrillation, which has not been recorded before.

Which underlying endocrine disorder should be tested for?
why_correct: Weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance and a fine tremor are classic features of thyrotoxicosis, which increases sympathetic sensitivity and atrial excitability and is a recognised cause of new atrial fibrillation, particularly in older people. Thyroid function is therefore part of the routine work-up of new atrial fibrillation, and treating the thyrotoxicosis often allows sinus rhythm to return. Source: Atrial fibrillation: causes, NHS website, 2025; Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023.
why_wrong: A. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia. C. Addison disease causes weight loss but with fatigue, pigmentation and hypotension rather than heat intolerance and tremor. D. Hyperparathyroidism causes thirst, constipation and bone pain rather than this picture. E. Cushing syndrome causes weight gain and central obesity.
pearl: Older people with hyperthyroidism may have few classic symptoms (apathetic thyrotoxicosis), so atrial fibrillation or weight loss may be the only clue.
thinking: New atrial fibrillation ↓ Weight loss with good appetite ↓ Heat intolerance and fine tremor ↓ Excess thyroid hormone ↓ Hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A, Hypothyroidism — both thyroid states disturb the heart, but underactivity slows the rate, whereas weight loss and heat intolerance point to overactivity.
takeaway: Check thyroid function in new atrial fibrillation, as hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause.

stem:
At the endocrine clinic, a 58-year-old man is reviewed after his GP found a suppressed TSH with a raised free T4. He has lost weight and feels jittery, and examination reveals a single firm lump in the left lobe of his thyroid. There are no eye signs. The team want to know whether this lump is the source of his excess hormone.

Which imaging test would best answer this?

options.D: Chest X-ray including the thoracic inlet
options.E: PET-CT of the neck and chest

why_correct: In a patient who is thyrotoxic with a nodule, the key question is whether the nodule itself is producing hormone. A radionuclide (technetium-99m pertechnetate or radioiodine) scan shows uptake, so a toxic adenoma appears as a 'hot' nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland. Hot nodules are very rarely malignant, which also guides whether further cytology is needed. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023.
why_wrong: A. CT gives anatomical detail only, and iodinated contrast can block thyroid uptake for weeks and delay radionuclide imaging or radioiodine treatment. B. MRI shows structure, not iodine uptake, so it cannot tell whether the lump is functioning. D. A chest film may show tracheal deviation or retrosternal extension but says nothing about function. E. PET-CT is not used to assess thyroid nodule function, and incidental thyroid uptake on PET needs separate work-up.
pearl: A hot nodule on uptake scanning is almost always benign, whereas a cold nodule needs ultrasound-guided assessment for malignancy.
thinking: Suppressed TSH with raised free T4 ↓ Single palpable thyroid nodule ↓ Question is whether the nodule is autonomous ↓ Function is shown by isotope uptake, not anatomy ↓ Radionuclide uptake scan
exam_trap: A, Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck — it sounds like thorough imaging, but it shows anatomy only and the iodine load can interfere with later isotope scanning and radioiodine therapy.
takeaway: To find out whether a thyroid nodule is overproducing hormone, use a radionuclide uptake scan.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman tells the practice nurse that for several weeks she has noticed white, milk-like fluid leaking from both nipples and staining her bra. Her youngest child is eight and she has not breastfed for years. There is no breast lump, redness or pain.

What is the correct medical term for her symptom?
why_correct: Galactorrhoea is the discharge of milk from the breast unrelated to pregnancy or breastfeeding. Bilateral milky discharge from several ducts is typical. It should prompt a pregnancy test, a medication review, a serum prolactin and thyroid function tests. Source: Primary care clinical referral criteria: nipple discharge and galactorrhoea, NHS Cornwall and Isles of Scilly, accessed 2026.
why_wrong: A. Mastalgia means breast pain, which she does not have. B. Mammary duct ectasia is a benign condition, usually after the menopause, causing a thick yellow, green or brown discharge from several ducts, not milk. D. Gynaecomastia is enlargement of male breast tissue. E. Mastitis is inflammation of the breast with pain, redness and warmth.
pearl: Common drug causes of galactorrhoea include antipsychotics such as risperidone and dopamine antagonists such as metoclopramide and domperidone.
thinking: Bilateral milky nipple discharge ↓ Not pregnant and not breastfeeding ↓ No inflammation or lump ↓ Inappropriate milk production ↓ Galactorrhoea
exam_trap: B, Mammary duct ectasia — it is a common benign cause of discharge from both breasts, but the discharge is thick and coloured rather than milky.
takeaway: Milk discharge outside pregnancy and breastfeeding is called galactorrhoea.

stem:
A 37-year-old woman with newly confirmed Graves disease phones the endocrine nurse helpline. She has started carbimazole but says her hands shake so much she cannot write and her heart races at night. She has no asthma and no heart failure. Her consultant has said full control of her thyroid will take several weeks.

Which medicine is most appropriate to ease these symptoms in the meantime?
why_correct: Many symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, including tremor, palpitations, sweating and anxiety, are driven by increased sensitivity to adrenergic stimulation. A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol relieves these quickly while antithyroid drugs take several weeks to lower hormone levels. It is contraindicated in asthma, which she does not have. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023; Overactive thyroid: treatment, NHS website, 2023.
why_wrong: A. Diazepam may reduce anxiety but does not treat the adrenergic tremor and tachycardia, and carries a dependence risk. B. Levothyroxine is thyroid hormone replacement and would worsen thyrotoxicosis unless used in a block-and-replace regimen. C. Digoxin is used for rate control in atrial fibrillation, but she has a sinus tachycardia and digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxic states. D. Amlodipine lowers blood pressure but does not control tremor or heart rate.
pearl: If a beta-blocker is contraindicated, a rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker such as diltiazem can be used for symptom control, usually on specialist advice.
thinking: New Graves disease on carbimazole ↓ Antithyroid drugs act slowly ↓ Tremor and palpitations are adrenergic ↓ No asthma so beta-blockade is safe ↓ Propranolol
exam_trap: C, Digoxin — it slows the heart in atrial fibrillation, but she has adrenergic sinus tachycardia and tremor, which a beta-blocker treats far better.
takeaway: Use a beta-blocker such as propranolol for adrenergic symptoms while waiting for antithyroid treatment to work.

stem:
Over the past month a 15-year-old girl's trousers have become loose, she is up repeatedly at night to pass urine and she carries a water bottle everywhere. Her mother brings her to the GP, where a fingerprick glucose is high and her urine shows ketones. She is slim and has no family history of diabetes.

What is the underlying cause of her condition?

options.A: Resistance of peripheral tissues to insulin
options.B: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.C: Overproduction of glucagon by a pancreatic tumour
options.D: Failure of ADH release from the pituitary
options.E: Excess cortisol production by the adrenal glands

correct_answer: B. Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
why_correct: Rapid weight loss, thirst and polyuria with hyperglycaemia and ketonuria in a slim teenager indicate type 1 diabetes. This results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, fat is broken down to ketones, which is why ketonuria is present, and she needs same-day specialist referral. Source: Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people: diagnosis and management (NG18), NICE, 2015, updated 2023.
why_wrong: A. Insulin resistance underlies type 2 diabetes, usually in older or overweight people without early ketosis. C. A glucagonoma is very rare and causes a characteristic rash with weight loss in adults. D. ADH deficiency causes dilute polyuria with normal glucose. E. Excess cortisol causes central weight gain, not rapid weight loss.
pearl: Suspected type 1 diabetes in a child or young person should be referred the same day to a paediatric diabetes team because of the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.
thinking: Slim teenager ↓ Weight loss, thirst and nocturia over weeks ↓ Hyperglycaemia with ketonuria ↓ Absolute insulin deficiency ↓ Autoimmune beta-cell destruction
exam_trap: A, Resistance of peripheral tissues to insulin — it explains type 2 diabetes, but ketosis and weight loss in a slim teenager point to absolute insulin deficiency.
takeaway: Type 1 diabetes results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells.

stem:
Over the past few months, a 57-year-old taxi driver has noticed he is passing urine more often and keeps a bottle of water in his cab. He has a BMI in the obese range, his mother developed diabetes in her sixties, and he has had two episodes of balanitis. Two HbA1c results taken a fortnight apart are both clearly in the diabetic range. Urine ketones are negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Gradual osmotic symptoms, recurrent genital candidal infection, obesity and a family history in a middle-aged adult, with two diagnostic HbA1c results and no ketosis, fit type 2 diabetes. Two abnormal results confirm the diagnosis in someone without acute hyperglycaemic illness. Source: Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk (PH38), NICE, 2012, updated 2017.
why_wrong: B. Type 1 diabetes usually presents more abruptly in a younger, slimmer person with weight loss and ketones. C. Diabetes insipidus does not raise HbA1c. D. Hyperparathyroidism can cause thirst and polyuria but not hyperglycaemia or balanitis. E. Cushing syndrome can cause hyperglycaemia but needs features such as proximal myopathy, striae and easy bruising, which are absent.
pearl: A single raised HbA1c or glucose is enough to diagnose diabetes only when the person has symptoms; without symptoms a second confirmatory test is needed.
thinking: Months of thirst and frequent urination ↓ Obesity and family history are risk factors ↓ Recurrent balanitis reflects glycosuria ↓ Two diagnostic HbA1c results, no ketones ↓ Gradual onset in a middle-aged adult fits type 2 diabetes
exam_trap: B, Type 1 diabetes mellitus — any adult with osmotic symptoms can have it, but the absence of ketones, gradual onset and strong type 2 risk profile make it far less likely.
takeaway: Gradual hyperglycaemic symptoms in an obese middle-aged adult with confirmed raised HbA1c and no ketones indicate type 2 diabetes.

stem:
At an NHS Health Check, a 45-year-old office worker asks which aspects of his lifestyle and health make diabetes more likely in his case. He walks to work, eats a mostly Mediterranean-style diet, but his waist circumference has increased steadily over the past decade.

Which feature most increases his risk of developing type 2 diabetes?

options.B: Diet high in fruit and vegetables
options.E: A body mass index in the low-normal range

why_correct: Excess body fat, particularly visceral fat around the abdomen, drives insulin resistance and is the most important modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes. A rising waist circumference is a strong marker of this risk even when other habits are healthy. Source: Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk (PH38), NICE, 2012, updated 2017.
why_wrong: A. Regular physical activity improves insulin sensitivity and lowers risk. B. A diet rich in fruit, vegetables and fibre is protective. D. High insulin sensitivity is the opposite of the insulin resistance that underlies type 2 diabetes. E. A low-normal BMI is associated with lower, not higher, risk.
pearl: People of South Asian, Chinese, African-Caribbean and Black African origin develop type 2 diabetes at lower BMI thresholds, so NICE uses lower BMI cut-offs to define overweight in these groups.
thinking: Asks about personal diabetes risk ↓ Healthy activity and diet are protective ↓ Waist size rising over years ↓ Visceral fat drives insulin resistance ↓ Central obesity is the key risk factor
exam_trap: D, High insulin sensitivity — the term sounds medical and relevant, but it describes a protective state; insulin resistance is what causes risk.
takeaway: Central obesity is the major modifiable risk factor for type 2 diabetes.

stem:
A 37-year-old office manager who does not have diabetes describes episodes of shakiness, clamminess and a racing heart that come on two to four hours after large pasta or bread-heavy lunches. The episodes never occur when fasting overnight and settle within minutes of eating a snack. She has had no gastric surgery.

Which condition best explains her symptoms?
why_correct: Adrenergic symptoms a few hours after a carbohydrate-rich meal, relieved by eating and never seen when fasting, suggest reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia, thought to reflect an exaggerated or delayed insulin response after the initial post-meal rise in glucose. Before the label is accepted, a low glucose should be documented during a typical episode (Whipple's triad), for example with a supervised mixed-meal test. Source: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycaemic disorders, Endocrine Society guideline 2009, summarised by the Association for Laboratory Medicine (UK), 2019.
why_wrong: A. Thyrotoxicosis causes persistent rather than meal-linked symptoms, with weight loss and heat intolerance. B. Phaeochromocytoma attacks are not tied to carbohydrate meals and include headache and hypertension. D. Insulinoma typically causes fasting hypoglycaemia, and her episodes never occur overnight. E. Panic disorder would not have such a consistent relation to meals or be relieved by food.
pearl: Postprandial hypoglycaemia is also seen after gastric surgery (late dumping), so ask about previous upper gastrointestinal operations including bariatric procedures.
thinking: No diabetes ↓ Adrenergic symptoms hours after high-carbohydrate meals ↓ Never fasting, relieved by food ↓ No previous gastric surgery ↓ Reactive hypoglycaemia
exam_trap: D, Insulinoma — it is the textbook cause of hypoglycaemia in someone without diabetes, but it characteristically causes fasting rather than post-meal episodes.
takeaway: Hypoglycaemic symptoms that follow carbohydrate meals and not fasting suggest reactive hypoglycaemia.

stem:
A 29-year-old man without diabetes keeps telling his GP that he has spells of sweating and feeling muddled which he believes are 'low sugar attacks' because a chocolate bar helps. Before arranging specialist tests, the GP wants to know what would confirm that genuine hypoglycaemia is occurring.

Which combination of findings is required?

options.A: Symptoms that consistently improve after eating, with no glucose measured
options.B: Symptoms, a low glucose measured during them, and relief with glucose
options.C: A low glucose on a single routine fasting sample, taken without any symptoms
options.D: Palpitations, headache and hypertension during attacks
options.E: Weight loss, thirst and polyuria over several weeks

correct_answer: B. Symptoms, a low glucose measured during them, and relief with glucose
why_correct: Whipple's triad confirms clinically significant hypoglycaemia: symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, a low plasma glucose measured during those symptoms, and resolution of symptoms once glucose is raised. All three elements are needed before investigating causes such as insulinoma. Source: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycaemic disorders, Endocrine Society guideline 2009, summarised by the Association for Laboratory Medicine (UK), 2019.
why_wrong: A. Feeling better after food is non-specific and does not prove a low glucose. C. An isolated low reading without symptoms may be artefactual or of no clinical significance. D. Headache, palpitations and hypertension suggest phaeochromocytoma. E. Weight loss, thirst and polyuria indicate hyperglycaemia rather than hypoglycaemia.
pearl: In suspected spontaneous hypoglycaemia, the definitive test is a supervised prolonged fast, measuring glucose, insulin, C-peptide and a sulfonylurea screen during a documented low.
thinking: Episodic symptoms attributed to low sugar ↓ Needs proof before investigation ↓ Symptoms must coincide with low glucose ↓ And resolve when glucose is corrected ↓ Whipple's triad
exam_trap: A, Symptoms that consistently improve after eating — this is what the patient reports, but without a measured low glucose it cannot confirm hypoglycaemia.
takeaway: Genuine hypoglycaemia is confirmed by Whipple's triad: symptoms, low measured glucose, and relief with glucose.

stem:
A 76-year-old retired miner who still smokes is admitted under the medical team after a fortnight of constipation, drinking more than usual and episodes of muddled thinking. He has lost weight without trying over the past two months. His adjusted calcium is markedly raised and his parathyroid hormone is suppressed.

Which underlying cause is most likely?
why_correct: A rapid onset of marked symptomatic hypercalcaemia, weight loss and smoking in an older adult, with a suppressed PTH, point to malignancy. Tumours raise calcium through PTH-related peptide (for example squamous cell lung cancer) or bone metastases and myeloma, and the suppressed PTH shows the parathyroids are not the cause. Source: Hypercalcaemia in adult patients in secondary care, NHS Scotland Right Decisions, 2022; Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients, Society for Endocrinology, 2016.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause overall but gives a raised or inappropriately normal PTH, not a suppressed one, and usually milder calcium. B. Thiazides cause only mild hypercalcaemia and he is not reported to take one. C. Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia is lifelong, mild and asymptomatic. D. Standard vitamin D supplements rarely cause marked hypercalcaemia, and he has no such history.
pearl: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy together account for about nine in ten cases of hypercalcaemia; measuring PTH is the key first step in separating them.
thinking: Older smoker with weight loss ↓ Constipation, thirst and confusion ↓ Marked hypercalcaemia ↓ PTH suppressed, so not parathyroid driven ↓ Malignancy is most likely
exam_trap: A, Primary hyperparathyroidism — it is the most common cause of a raised calcium, but a suppressed PTH and rapid, severe symptoms with weight loss point to cancer.
takeaway: Marked hypercalcaemia with suppressed PTH and weight loss in an older adult should be treated as malignancy until proven otherwise.
